patient.name: Claudette Fontaine
patient.chief_complaint: Progressive bilateral lower extremity weakness and sensory loss with recent right thigh pain, 14 months
patient.hpi: Claudette Fontaine is a 46-year-old legal secretary with a 14-month history of progressive bilateral lower extremity symptoms that have followed an unusual course compared to typical neuropathy. She describes the onset as acute severe right anterior thigh and groin pain 14 months ago — so severe she presented to the ED and was evaluated for a femoral hernia (negative) and kidney stone (negative). Over the following weeks, she developed profound right thigh and leg weakness and was unable to climb stairs on the right. Over the next 6 months, left lower extremity symptoms developed in a mirror pattern: left anterior thigh pain followed by left leg weakness. Simultaneously, she has lost approximately 7 kg without trying and has been working up her weight loss with her primary care physician. She was eventually diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 6 months ago (HbA1c 8.4%) and her primary care physician attributed the neuropathy to diabetes. However, the acute onset of unilateral thigh pain and asymmetric progression troubles her current neurologist. Her current symptoms include bilateral leg weakness (right > left), persistent right anterior thigh and knee pain, difficulty climbing stairs and rising from chairs, and mild distal foot numbness. She denies alcohol use. She does not take metformin (started glipizide 3 months ago).

emg.summary: ACUTE SEVERE LUMBOSACRAL PLEXOPATHY BILATERALLY (right >> left). Femoral territory predominant (rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, iliacus). Paraspinal involvement at L2-L4. Distal muscles relatively preserved. NOT consistent with typical length-dependent distal polyneuropathy.

report.overall_impression: SEVERELY ABNORMAL NCS/EMG — acute lumbosacral radiculoplexopathy pattern. Severely reduced right femoral motor amplitude with markedly prolonged distal latency. Left femoral motor mildly reduced. Right saphenous sensory severely reduced; left mildly reduced. Distal nerve conduction studies relatively preserved. EMG: 4+ acute denervation (fibrillations, PSW) in right rectus femoris and vastus lateralis; 3+ in right iliacus; 2+ in left quadriceps muscles. Paraspinal involvement at L2-L4 bilaterally. Nascent/reduced MUPs in proximal muscles. Pattern localizes to the lumbosacral radiculoplexus level, proximal and predominantly femoral territory, right greater than left. Findings are not consistent with length-dependent distal polyneuropathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

results.citation: Dyck PJB et al. (2001) Inflammatory vasculopathy in multifocal diabetic neuropathy. Ann Neurol 50:73-81.
results.summary: DLRPN pathophysiology: inflammatory microvasculitis of epineurial vessels causing ischemic injury to lumbosacral plexus. Immune-mediated mechanism. Case series: IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day x3 then oral taper associated with faster pain resolution and trend toward improved strength. IVIG for severe cases.

results.citation: Krendel DA et al. (1995) Immunopathology of diabetic plexopathy. Muscle Nerve 18:1234-1239.
results.summary: Pain management: pregabalin 150-300 mg twice daily (neuropathic pain), amitriptyline 10-25 mg nightly (sleep), opioids for severe acute phase. Physical therapy essential during recovery phase. Recovery often takes 12-24 months; incomplete in 30-50% of patients.

output.impression: Physical Therapy Assessment — DLRPN Rehabilitation PT assessment: Right quadriceps severe atrophy (circumference deficit 2 cm). Hip flexor weakness bilateral. Trendelenburg bilateral. Berg Balance Scale 38/56 — significant fall risk. Functional Mobility Assessment: unable to rise from low chair independently. Recommendations: (1) Passive ROM phase: gentle passive stretching, aquatic therapy if available, (2) Active phase when strength >3/5: progressive resistive exercises for quadriceps and hip flexors, (3) Balance and proprioception training, (4) Knee-ankle-foot orthosis (KAFO) for right leg if knee buckling risk. Home exercise program provided. Significant rehabilitation needs. DLRPN recovery is slow — physical therapy must begin early to prevent secondary contractures, disuse atrophy, and falls. Aquatic therapy is preferred in acute phase (supported ambulation). Standardized balance assessment reveals a significant fall risk (Berg Balance Scale 38/56). Bilateral hip flexor and knee extensor weakness with bilateral Trendelenburg sign. Right quadriceps severe atrophy with a 2 cm circumference deficit. Patient is unable to rise independently from a low chair. Functional mobility is substantially impaired, predominantly by proximal lower extremity weakness

Repeat NCS/EMG (6 months post-diagnosis) Repeat NCS/EMG at 6 months: Right femoral motor amplitude 1.8 mV (from 0.4 mV — significantly improved). Left femoral motor amplitude 3.4 mV (from 1.8 mV — improved). Rectus femoris EMG: fibrillations 2+ (from 4+ — reducing). Nascent MUPs appearing in right rectus femoris (early reinnervation). Saphenous SNAP recovering bilaterally. Early reinnervation at 6 months — favorable prognostic sign. Right femoral motor amplitude improved 4.5x. Clinical correlation: patient can now rise from a standard chair without arm support (previously unable). Physical therapy to continue intensively through reinnervation phase. Interval improvement compared to prior study. Right femoral motor CMAP amplitude increased to 1.8 mV (from 0.4 mV); left femoral motor amplitude 3.4 mV (from 1.8 mV). Rectus femoris fibrillation potential density reduced (2+ from 4+); nascent motor unit potentials present in right rectus femoris, indicating early reinnervation. Bilateral saphenous SNAP amplitudes recovering. Findings are consistent with early axonal reinnervation in the lumbosacral radiculoplexus distribution

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy (DLRPN / Bruns-Garland syndrome)

differential.key_features: Same phenotype; need ANCA, ANA, biopsy if asymmetric/non-resolving — distinguished only by lack of diabetes or by inflammation on biopsy.
Asymmetric demyelinating CIDP; needs NCS for conduction block, CSF, and trial of IVIG.

differential.diagnosis: Lumbosacral spine structural disease (stenosis, mass, leptomeningeal disease)
differential.key_features: Bilateral progressive proximal weakness with weight loss should prompt imaging; pattern here is more peripheral than radicular.
Weight loss raises concern; need malignancy screen.
Does not explain acute pain, asymmetry, or proximal predominance.

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identify reversible/treatable etiologies (diabetes, B12 deficiency, monoclonal gammopathy, thyroid disease)

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Length-dependent axonal vs demyelinating vs multifocal pattern; severity and distribution

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identify potentially neurotoxic drugs (chemotherapy, metronidazole, megadose B6, nitrofurantoin); guide neuropathic-pain pharmacotherapy

optimal_actions.action: Vasculitis + paraneoplastic serologies and ESR/CRP given asymmetric proximal-predominant pattern
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identify or exclude vasculitic neuropathy and paraneoplastic causes (Sjögren's, ANCA, anti-Hu)

optimal_actions.action: Lumbosacral MRI (with contrast) to exclude structural radiculopathy / mass / leptomeningeal disease
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Rule out structural compression, neoplastic infiltration; in DLRPN may show enlarged enhancing lumbosacral plexus/roots

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated protein, normal cell count) supports CIDP

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is a cortical test and is non-contributory in peripheral nerve disease.
Head/brain CT has no role in peripheral neuropathy evaluation.
Advanced cerebral imaging (PET/MRA/MRV/perfusion) has no routine role in peripheral neuropathy.
Echocardiography is not indicated unless cardiac amyloid is suspected.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated unless there is syncope or symptomatic dysautonomia with arrhythmia concern.

sequence_constraints.reason: Tier the workup — basic labs first, then targeted electrodiagnostic and tissue studies.

critical_actions: Recognize the Bruns-Garland phenotype: acute proximal-predominant asymmetric leg pain and weakness + weight loss + new T2DM
Imaging of the lumbosacral plexus / spine to exclude structural / neoplastic causes
Glycemic optimization (does not reverse DLRPN but prevents progression)
Symptomatic pain control and intensive physical therapy
Counsel that recovery is slow (months to years) but generally favorable
contraindicated_actions: Do not delay imaging — structural and neoplastic causes must be excluded
Do not assume distal symmetric polyneuropathy when the pattern is asymmetric and proximal
key_reasoning_points: Diabetic LSRPN (Bruns-Garland) is a microvasculitic ischemic process of the lumbosacral plexus and roots
Hallmarks: acute pain, proximal weakness, weight loss, often with newly diagnosed or poorly controlled diabetes
Imaging excludes structural cause; some advocate IV methylprednisolone for severe disease

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Distal symmetric DM polyneuropathy does not cause acute proximal-predominant asymmetric weakness; DLRPN is the diabetic mimic.
Weight loss is a recognized feature of DLRPN itself; malignancy screen is still warranted but typical pattern + uncontrolled DM fits Bruns-Garland.
